bites.title: Docker images and Docker Compose
bites.body:
A **Docker image** packages your application code, its exact Python or Node runtime, system libraries and dependencies into a single self-contained snapshot. **Docker Compose** lets you define and run multi-container setups (such as your FastAPI backend, a Postgres + pgvector database and a Redis queue worker) together with one command (`docker compose up`). Check the current details in the Docker documentation.

Without containers, you hit the classic "it works on my laptop" failure when the production server has a different Python version or a missing PDF parsing library.

It is packing a whole mobile kitchen into a shipping container so every pan and stove is in the exact same place wherever the lorry parks.
bites.sourceNote: Drafted by AI, November 2026 · fast-moving topic, check current details · confidence: medium

questions.prompt: What problem do Docker images and Docker Compose solve for AI applications?

choices.text: They package the exact runtime, system libraries and supporting services together so the app runs identically on every machine
They make language models ten times smarter without changing the prompt
They eliminate the need to pay cloud hosting bills
They automatically write unit tests for your prompts

questions.explanation: Containerisation eliminates environment drift between laptops, test servers and cloud production.

bites.title: Packaging agents so they run anywhere
bites.body:
Once your agent service is packaged as a standard container image with a clear `Dockerfile`, you are no longer locked into a single hosting company.

That exact same container can run on your laptop today, on a cheap virtual server tomorrow, on AWS ECS or Google Cloud Run next month, or inside a corporate client's private Azure network next quarter. For an AI consultant, delivering a clean containerised service means the client's IT team can deploy and run your work using their standard tools without learning AI-specific quirks.

It is a standard mains plug that fits any wall socket in the country, regardless of who wired the building.
bites.sourceNote: Drafted by AI, November 2026 · confidence: high

questions.prompt: Why is packaging an agent service as a standard Docker container especially helpful in client consulting work?

choices.text: The client's IT team can deploy the container on whichever cloud or private server they already use without custom machine setup
Docker containers do not need any CPU or RAM to run
Containers bypass all corporate firewall rules automatically
A Dockerfile replaces the need for source code

questions.explanation: A clean container image gives you portable deployment across any cloud provider or client-hosted environment.

bites.title: Environment variables and secrets kept outside the image
bites.body:
Never hard-code API keys (`OPENAI_API_KEY`, `ANTHROPIC_API_KEY`, database passwords) in your source code or bake them into a Docker image with `COPY .env`.

Anyone who pulls that image or reads its layer history can extract your secret keys in seconds. Instead, build the image with code only, and inject configuration and secrets at **runtime** through environment variables supplied by your cloud secret manager (such as AWS Secrets Manager, Google Secret Manager or Azure Key Vault). Add `.env` to both `.gitignore` and `.dockerignore`.

It is building a safe with the combination set at installation by the owner, rather than painting the code on the door at the factory.
bites.sourceNote: Drafted by AI, November 2026 · confidence: high

questions.prompt: How should API keys and database passwords be passed to a containerised AI service?

choices.text: Injected at runtime via environment variables from a secret manager, never baked into the Docker image or committed to Git
Written directly at the top of `main.py` so they are easy to find
Copied into the Docker image during `docker build` and pushed to Docker Hub
Sent in the URL query string of every user request

questions.explanation: Keeping secrets in runtime environment variables prevents leaks through Git repositories or container registries and lets you rotate keys without rebuilding.

bites.title: The same container in testing and production
bites.body:
In a healthy deployment pipeline, you build the Docker image once from a specific Git commit hash (for example, `myapp:3ab783c`), run your automated unit and evaluation tests against that exact image in staging, and then promote that **exact same image** to production by changing only its environment variables.

If you rebuild from scratch in production with unpinned dependencies (`pip install langchain`), a library update released five minutes ago can silently break production even though staging passed.

It is testing a batch of medicine in the lab and shipping bottles from that exact tested batch, not mixing a new batch on the lorry.
bites.sourceNote: Drafted by AI, November 2026 · confidence: high

questions.prompt: Why should you promote the exact same built container image from testing to production rather than rebuilding it with unpinned dependencies?

choices.text: So you know the exact code and library versions that passed your tests are what runs in production, with no surprise package updates
Because building an image twice costs a million pounds
Because production servers cannot run `pip install`
So that test database data is copied to real customers

questions.explanation: Pinning dependencies in lockfiles and promoting the tested image artifact guarantees that production matches what passed staging.
